newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria says democracy timetable still intact.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria says democracy timetable still intact.

text.p: Postponement of local elections in Nigeria has raised new doubts about the military's commitment to restoring full democracy by 1998, but the electoral commission said the target date remained in force.
On Sunday the electoral commission NECON and the political parties said that municipal elections which should have been held by the end of this month would now take place by March.
Registration and production of a voters' list were also supposed to be completed this month. In practice, none of these has been accomplished.
Opposition groups have yet to react, but are bound to point to the vote postponement as evidence that Nigeria's military rulers are not serious about handing power to an elected government.
Lagos-based diplomats said the postponement did not help to convey an impression that the authorities are in earnest about restoring democracy.
"Key items of the transition programme are outstanding, which suggests that NECON has not done much to show it is serious about the transition," said one senior Western diplomat.
The municipal elections are aimed at testing the strength of the five political parties allowed to register three months ago.

NECON and the parties agreed at a meeting in the capital Abuja on Sunday to shift them to early next year along with the remaining activities of the transition programme that should have been undertaken this year.
"Such activities would be concluded between the 10th of February and the 31st of March 1997," said a statement signed by the electoral commission NECON and the political parties.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, plunged into crisis in June 1993 when the the previous military ruler annulled a presidential election to choose his successor.
Moshood Abiola, the undeclared winner of the annulled poll is in detention for proclaiming himself president and his supporters insist he should be freed and installed president.
Nigeria came under renewed pressure last year to restore democracy when it defied world opinion and hanged nine minority rights activists including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa for murder.
General Sani Abacha, who seized power in the chaos of 1993 last year, launched a plan to restore civilian rule by October 1998, which the opposition and the West criticised as too long.

"The meeting recognised that as much as these changes have become necessary, they do not negate the basic objective of the transition programme, which terminal date remains 1st October, 1998," the joint statement of the electoral commission and the political parties said.
"(The electoral commission) would publish an appropriate programme of activities to include the carryover activities along with those earlier scheduled for the 1st quarter 1997."
NECON blames the delay on the creation of six new states and 183 local council areas last October.
"The creation of new states and new local governments meant we had to plan all over the process of delineating constituencies and voters' registration," said a NECON official.
